news.title: Key oddity of quantum physics may run even deeper than anticipated
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print We are still searching for a non-probabilistic understanding of quantum mechanics Photo by H. Armstrong Roberts/ClassicStock/Getty Images Quantum mechanics’ probabilistic nature has puzzled researchers for more than a century.

A new analysis shows that ridding the theory of this odd characteristic may be even harder than anticipated. Left undisturbed and isolated, the cat remains mixed, but if it is observed – if an experimenter opens its box, say – it abruptly reduces to just one, unmixed state. How exactly this happens – a question known as the measurement problem – is among the biggest unresolved questions about quantum mechanics.

news.title: Dinosaur named after fossil-loving dad from Surrey
paras: A new species of dinosaur has been named after a dad who worked in the building where it was found in Surrey, in the south of England. William Proudlove was a manager of the Ewhurst brick and tile works, and was very interested in fossils himself.

An ancient dino fossil was found there in 2001 and donated to the Natural History Museum, who have recently looked at the fossil again and realised it's actually a brand new species. news.title: Building boom puts 300,000 people in the path of potential Himalayan disasters
paras: At least 300,000 people in parts of the Himalayan region could now be living in the path of potential disasters, a new study suggests. Researchers found that the amount of built-up land in high-risk zones in northern Nepal, parts of south-eastern Tibet and a corner of India's Uttarakhand had grown by about 45% between 2016 and 2023.

In areas particularly threatened by flooding from glacial lakes, development increased even faster, rising by almost 78% over the same period, according to the peer-reviewed study published in Scientific Reports. The team of scientists behind it said the true number of people under threat could be much higher, as they only analysed a specific territory and not neighbouring areas which face similar risks.

sport.title: How Far Has Andrey Rublev Really Fallen?
paras: October 29, 2026 By Jack Beatnik ATP , Opinion How Far Has Andrey Rublev Really Fallen? He was not necessarily winning Grand Slams, but he was winning an awful lot of tennis matches. Now, at 29, Rublev finds himself increasingly removed from the sport’s elite.

But has his tennis actually deteriorated as much as his ranking suggests? Interestingly, the numbers provide a slightly more complicated answer. Rublev has won more than 60% of his matches this season, which includes a title in Bastad and reached another two finals. Those hardly sound like the results of a player experiencing a complete collapse but when compared with his best years, the differences become rather difficult to ignore.
